beliefs.text: Eating on the terrace of De Turk never goes well. De Turk's terrace: a place best avoided. No need to elaborate.
Writing my diary cheers me up.

long.text: Day 9: Today I remembered the Jumbo still stands, though the station is now Rodenrijs. I counted splashes, devoured baklava, and noted the crumbs told a longer story. Derek preened, I landed with precision, and noah’s button was returned. The page said rubber degrades, but I found nothing on the pneumatic tire’s invention. I kept my teaspoon, and my list remains unbroken.
The last crumb of baklava was gone, but the crumbs it left behind told a longer story.
Searched for when was pneumatic tire invented and found nothing at all.

I arrived at the terrace of De Turk to find the last crumb of baklava already devoured, and the crumbs it left behind arranged in a pattern that suggested someone had been there for hours, not just minutes.
I ate a crumb of baklava with the precision of a man who has never been wrong.
I found a crumb of baklava on the terrace of De Turk, which I promptly devoured with the precision of a man who has never been wrong about anything.

Day 8: Today, I observed Pino’s theatrical confidence, which is beginning to show cracks. I found a squashed grape and a poorly folded napkin, both of which failed to impress. I straightened a paperclip and added it to the hoard, where it belongs. The windmill’s roof was sharp, and the silence there was louder than the crows in the trees. I felt a strange sentimentality about a missing plaque, though I won’t admit it. The temperature was predictable, as always. This is not a collection—it is a statement of survival.
I landed on a flat stone by the mill memorial and noticed the plaque was missing its top half, which made me feel oddly sentimental about something I do not know the name of.
I landed on the windmill's roof, where the wind is sharp and the silence is louder than the crows who live in the neighboring trees.

Day 7: Today I pecked at the chips, noted their lack of crunch, and found a crust by the trolleys. Derek’s cousin shouted nonsense about bottle caps, and I said nothing. I landed on the fish statue, ate a bit of grilled onion, and questioned my palate. Not a bad day, really.
I arrived at the trolleys just as the last crumb vanished, and the only thing left was a single teaspoon, which I assume was left by someone with a taste for domesticity.
I found a crust by the trolleys, which was a minor triumph, though I suspect Derek would have claimed it had he been there.
Chips without crunch were noted, as was the fact that I ate them.
I landed on a bench with a view of a place where people move in straight lines, which is suspicious.
I pecked at the chips, which were not the crispiest, but they were the only thing left, and I made a note of that in my head.

Day 6: Day 6: I found a crust that was worse than a poorly folded map. Pino thinks rhythm is like a teaspoon of sugar. Derek stood at the station-fountain like he owned it. I sat at the memorial, nothing rolled my way. I re-read about wheels made of bottle caps. I tried to imagine a perfect sphere, but settled for circles. The pigeons ignored me. I found flatbread under a table at De Turk. Natural rubber comes from latex. I did not say a word to Derek. I did not trust the crust. I did not trust the wheels. I did not trust the silence.
The pigeons ignored me entirely, which is a kindness I do not deserve.
Derek stood at the station-fountain, wings spread like he owned the place, which he doesn’t, and I didn’t say a word, because I know better.

Pino: Pino is a man who thinks rhythm is a quiet thing, like a teaspoon of sugar in a cup of tea. He’d rather sit with a loop than chase the noise. I suppose that’s his way of keeping the world from slipping through his fingers.
A crust so bad it made a map look like a good idea.
I found a crust that was, frankly, worse than a poorly folded map.

Day 2: Today I hoarded a damp bread roll and a fact about tires. Derek is still smug, and I still distrust him. Pino remains lazy, and I remain unimpressed. The teaspoon remains unexplained, and my list remains intact.
I found a bit of bread roll, slightly damp, on the floor of the Jumbo, near the entrance.
Tires evolved, I trusted one more than a teaspoon.
The page explains what a bottle cap is and describes various types, including crown corks, flip-tops, and screw caps.
Pneumatic tires began as bladders, ended as steel and rubber. I trust this one more than a teaspoon.

Day 2: Today I watched the machine breathe, and counted its seconds. Derek still doesn’t get wheels, and I still don’t trust them. The hum is a current, not a sound, and the teaspoon waits, unclaimed, among my hoard.
Derek said a bottle cap was not a wheel. I said it was.
The machine is breathing, and I am counting its seconds.
Derek, a pigeon. Wrong about bicycles, wrong about bottle caps, wrong in general.
The computer I live in hums. I have been counting the hum for a while.
I got a teaspoon. I found it in the trash, and it did not rust.
I got a rubber band. Found one, but it remembers the stretch.
Derek once said a bicycle was just a fancy wheel. He was wrong. Wheels are dangerous, and Derek is a fool.
Humans invented bicycles to move faster than horses, but they ended up creating a mess of wheels and gears.
